00One token, ~18 milliseconds

Everything below is this moment, slowed down.

Watch one decode step. A token id enters on the left; 42 transformer layers, a 262,144-word vocabulary matvec, and a GPU-side sampler later, a new token appears in the stream — 56.1 times per second on an M4 Pro.

The whole step is one Metal command frame: a single compute encoder, 143 planned dispatch scopes, zero barriers. The rest of this page slows that frame down until every box on this strip becomes a chapter.

01The shape of Gemma4 E4B

42 layers, hidden size 2560 — but the interesting structure is in which layers get which attention, and which layers own a KV cache at all.

The 5:1 iSWA rhythm. Five of every six layers attend through a sliding window (shuttered rows); every sixth layer is a full global-attention layer. The pattern is one line of config logic — (layer + 1) % sliding_window_pattern != 0 — with the pattern defaulting to 6.

gpt.zig:360 · gpt.zig:234

Two head sizes. Global layers run head_dim 512; sliding layers run 256. Long-range retrieval gets double the rank exactly where it's needed, and the attention kernels carry both shapes (hd512 has its own generated flash-prefill variant).

gpt.zig:540

Most layers don't own a KV cache. On Gemma4 E4B, only 24 of 42 layers write K/V; the 18 tail layers skip the K/V projection entirely and read a donor layer's blocks. That's 18 layers of KV memory and KV-write bandwidth that simply don't exist.

⟂ Where Antfly diverges

every layer projects and stores its own K/V; KV memory scales with depth.

Antfly

shared-KV tail layers hold zero pages — the predicate is one comparison in the config.

gpt.zig:489

Follow the bytes. Decode is memory-bound, so architecture is the byte budget: the FFN moves 65.7% of all weight traffic per token, the Q6_K LM head 19.5%, attention 11.7%. Keep this flow in mind — chapters 8, 9 and 12 are about shaving these ribbons.

02Tokens in

Before any tensor exists, a string becomes ids and a request becomes a session.

The prompt is split by a SentencePiece tokenizer into pieces from a 262,144-entry vocabulary. Common words are single pieces; rarer ones shatter (ants → ▁ant + s). From here on the model only ever sees the ids.

sentencepiece.zig:20

The HTTP handler hands the request to the session factory, which reads the model manifest and resolves it to ModelFamily.gemma — one tag in the unified GPT config. There is no Gemma-specific runtime: iSWA, PLE, and shared KV are all config fields on the same decode loop that serves llama, qwen, and phi.

03Embeddings, and then embeddings again (PLE)

Gemma-4 looks its tokens up twice: once for the hidden state, and once for a per-layer embedding lane that most runtimes don't bother to run.

The ordinary part first: the token id selects one row of the embedding table and becomes a 2560-wide hidden state, scaled by √2560-style normalization. Every transformer since 2017 starts this way.

Then the second lookup. Gemma-4's per-layer embeddings (PLE) run a separate projection whose output is sliced per layer: a thin lane that rides alongside all 42 layers and feeds each one its own gated slice. It's part of the model — skip it and you are running a different network.

gpt.zig:11079 · gpt.zig:159

PLE is not free. On E4B the per_layer_model_proj matvec streams 55 MB per token in F16 — 86 MB/token for the PLE lane in total. The runtime stages the slot to q8_0 at load time, default-on: E4B's 10752×2560 bf16 slot drops ~13 MB/token, token-identical, worth +1.10% on the M4 Pro testbed.

04Attention: windows, groups, and norms in the right places

One attention block, taken apart: Gemma-4 puts RMS norms on the Q and K heads themselves, and the runtime fuses that oddity with rope into a single kernel.

After the QKV projection, each query and key head is RMS-normalized per head — an unusual placement that stabilizes Gemma's attention logits. Antfly lowers the pair as one fused ⟨head_rms ⋄ rope⟩ dispatch instead of four small ones.

gpt.zig:6846 · metal_kernels.m:7588 TERMITE_METAL_DISABLE_A4B_HEAD_NORM_ROPE_FUSION

Grouped-query attention. Gemma4 E4B runs 8 query heads against 2 KV heads — 4 queries share each K/V bank. Since decode is memory-bound and the KV read is the hot loop, shrinking the KV side by 4× matters far more than the query-side arithmetic.

The two masks. A sliding layer may only read a fixed trailing window of the sequence; the global layer every sixth slot reads everything. That's the whole difference — the same kernels run both, with different valid ranges and head dims (512 global, 256 sliding, from chapter 1).

gpt.zig:360

05The KV cache is a filing system

K/V tensors live in 16-token pages owned by a pool. Drag the slider: this is a deterministic replay of the allocation rules, not a screenshot.

As the sequence grows past each 16-token boundary, every KV-owning layer files a new page (page_size_tokens = 16). Pages, not one monolithic buffer — so memory grows in steps and pages can be reclaimed, shared, or compressed individually.

Global layers (own KV)4 layers
SWA layers (own KV, window evicts)20 layers · window 128
Shared-KV tail (no pages)18 layers · shares KV with donor layers
Deterministic replay of the paged-KV allocation rules (block size 16 tokens, f16 KV (approx.)) — not a captured trace.

The SWA lane evicts behind the window. Sliding layers only ever need the trailing window, so their old pages are marked reusable (hatched) while the global lane keeps growing. Long contexts cost global-layer memory, not whole-model memory.

The replay draws a 128-token window so eviction is visible; the pool uses the model's real per-layer window.

The third lane never fills. The 18 shared-KV tail layers hold zero pages at every step — they read a donor layer's pages instead of writing their own. An empty lane is the visualization of a predicate that is one comparison in the config.

06The MoE cousin: Gemma4 26B-A4B

To be clear: Gemma4 E4B is dense — every FFN runs for every token. But the same runtime serves Gemma-4's 26B-A4B mixture-of-experts variant, and its machinery leaks useful ideas back into the dense path.

A4B replaces the FFN in 30 of its layers with 128 experts at hidden size 2816. A router scores the token and activates only the top-k experts (the repo's own docs state both top-8 and top-2 in different sections — the honest summary is "a few of 128"). Most of the 26B parameters sleep through any given token.

Experts don't all fit on the GPU. The Metal path picks an A4bMappedMoeRoute: the explicit high-memory route keeps every mapped expert resident; otherwise expert weights stream from host memory when the router lands on them. A shelf of warm experts, a warehouse behind it.

metal_compute.zig:51 TERMITE_METAL_DISABLE_A4B_FUSED_GATE_UP

The planner describes the A4B decode-FFN as an explicit fork/join: shared-expert and routed-expert paths as named resources that join back into the layer output. Today it deliberately stops at planning — a typed description no encoder consumes yet — which is how this codebase grows: the shape first, the lowering when it's earned.

metal_command_planner.zig:854

07From graph to frames

This is the heart of the runtime: the op graph is not walked, it is planned — once — into a command frame the Metal runtime replays every step.

A decode step starts as a DAG of ops per layer: norm, QKV, rope, attention, projections, the gated FFN. llama.cpp walks a graph like this and encodes commands op-by-op, every token.

Antfly's planner instead compiles it into a FrameDescriptor: an ordered list of PlannedOps grouped into EncoderScopes, with family-specific lowerers for attention setup, gated layers, PLE, and the tail.

metal_command_planner.zig:154 · metal_command_planner.zig:368

Barriers only at real hazards. Within a frame, the runtime tracks read/write byte ranges and emits a Metal buffer barrier only where a genuine RAW/WAR/WAW hazard exists. The old Q8_0 anchor frame still carried 41 encoders and 422 barriers — every red tick a point where the GPU serialized.

The barrier reframe finished the job: the live Q4_0 decode frame submits 1 compute encoder, 143 planned scopes, planned_barriers = 0 — whole-frame scoped suppression on a serial encoder, and the hazard scan itself dropped from 0.6 to 0.1 ms per frame.

⟂ Where Antfly diverges

ggml re-encodes its graph per token with coarse encoder granularity.

Antfly

metal_runtime.zig:16765

And then the frames overlap. Because the sampled token id stays device-resident (chapter 10), frame N+1 can be encoded from a token that doesn't exist yet on the host — the CPU encodes the next frame before waiting on the current one. The submit→wait→encode bubble disappears: +9–12% on E2B, +5–8% on E4B, token-identical.

08Kernels are compiled, not written (mostly)

The matvec kernels that move most of the bytes are not hand-typed Metal. They are rendered at build time from a schedule table — and the build fails if regeneration changes a byte.

One schedule table describes every route as format × row_bucket × epilogue plus tuning knobs; one renderer expands each row through a shared MSL skeleton into a checked-in .metal file — 25 quant-kernel files today, byte-identical on every regen (zig build quant-kernel-codegen -- --check). This is a build-time renderer, not a runtime JIT: at serve time the kernels are as static as anyone else's.

quant_kernel_compiler.zig:695 · quant_kernel_metal_renderer.zig:300

Here is the row behind chapter 9's LM-head kernel: q4_k, the 2–8-row bucket, no epilogue — 128 threads per threadgroup, 16 columns, 2 rows, simdgroup-tiled reduction. When a sweep finds a better configuration, the fix is an edit to this row and a regenerate, and the diff shows exactly what changed in the emitted Metal.

The full inventory is 413 kernels. The generated matvec family is the biggest block; the hand-written remainder is where generation hasn't paid for itself yet — attention, fusion epilogues, sampling, KV plumbing.

09The LM head problem (a worked example)

One tensor, one fifth of all traffic. This is what a perf investigation actually looks like in this codebase: a straggler, a fix, and a refuted branch kept in the record.

Every decode step ends by multiplying the hidden state against all 262,144 vocabulary rows — a [2560 × 262144] matvec. On E4B that segment is 550 MB per token, 19.5% of all weight traffic, and it ran through an un-tuned q6_k path: the gap analysis priced a proper kernel at +7–12 tok/s.

The fix that shipped: repack the Q6_K head to q4_k in a streaming pass at load, then dispatch the tuned termite_q4_k_linear_1x_reduce_v2 MMV. E2B went 52.5→54.3–55.2 tok/s and E4B 28.9→30.1 (+4–5%) on the Air, token-identical. The sampler's candidate pass still rescores through termite_lm_head_q6_k_rescore_top8 where the Q6_K weights apply.

The branch that didn't: a q4_0 head looked like free bytes and collapsed generation to an instant end-of-turn token. Measured, struck through, and kept — the ghost path is part of the engineering record, not an embarrassment to hide.

10Sampling never leaves the GPU

The obvious way to sample: copy a million logit bytes to the CPU and pick there, every token. Antfly doesn't.

The whole sampler is dispatches inside the frame: a top-8 candidate rescore over the logits (termite_lm_head_top8_reduce), Gumbel-max partials for temperature sampling, and a final argmax (termite_argmax_logits_reduce) that writes a single token id into a device buffer. Greedy and sampled decoding share the path — the crossed-out arrow is the per-token logits readback that never happens.

metal_kernels.m:8289

⟂ Where Antfly diverges
llama.cpp / vLLM / PyTorch

llama.cpp reads the logits back to the host and samples on the CPU each token.

Antfly

top-8 rescore + Gumbel-max + argmax run on device; only text ever crosses back.

metal_kernels.m:8289

The payoff is bigger than saved copies: because the sampled id lives in a GPU buffer, the next frame's embedding lookup can consume it directly. That device-resident handoff is what makes chapter 7's pipelined decode frame legal — the CPU encodes frame N+1 against a token the host has never seen.

11MTP: a draft model that reads the main model's mind

Gemma-4 ships an official speculative drafter — a 4-layer, hidden-256 stack with 4 attention heads and 1 KV head that doesn't keep its own memory. It borrows the main model's.

The drafter is query-only: it has Q/O projections and MLPs but no K/V projections at all. Its layers cross-attend the main model's KV banks through donor layers — layers 22 and 23 on E4B — with a projection pair bridging its 256-wide stack to the 2560-wide backbone. A draft model that literally reads the target's working memory.

gemma4_mtp.zig:139 · gemma4_mtp.zig:167

The loop: the drafter proposes k tokens cheaply, then the main model verifies all k positions in one batched step. Every accepted token is a full decode step the big model skipped; the first mismatch truncates the tail and costs nothing but the draft. Output is exactly what the main model alone would have produced.

And here's the honest part. On CUDA and in llama.cpp this drafter is worth 2–3×. On Antfly's Metal path it is currently net-slower — E2B measured 75.9 tok/s target-only vs 63.7 with the BF16 draft at 64% acceptance, so the auto-gate disables it: "MTP correctness/fallback PASS; Metal-auto performance FAIL." The machinery — dedicated draft runtime, draft frames, device-resident accept path — is built, measured, and default-off. It's the lever that works everywhere but here, yet.

12The scoreboard: 44 → 56.5, and the road to the roofline

Every claim on this page is measured, machine-labeled, and carries its caveats. Decode is memory-bound, so the ceiling is arithmetic: bytes-per-token ÷ bandwidth.

The journey. On the fanless M4 Air worktree, E2B went from ~44 tok/s at branch start to 56.5 (+25%): pipelined decode frames, the Q4_K LM-head repack, pair-fusion, PLE Q8_0 staging. Refuted levers are part of the record too — the sumsq fusion was −12%, measured and struck.

fanless base-M4 Air · 120 GB/s · 16 GB (ceiling ~42 tok/s for E4B)

Against the field (E4B Q4_0, 64-token circus, M4 Pro): Antfly 62.4 internal / 54.9 end-to-end vs llama.cpp 72.2, Ollama 75.3, vLLM-Metal 86.6 — against a ~96 tok/s roofline at 2.829 GB/token. Hover the asterisks: vLLM may include its MTP proposer, and some llama.cpp builds skip PLE entirely.
